name: Crest Whitestrips
lead: Crest Whitestrips are over-the-counter teeth-whitening strips made by Procter & Gamble under the Crest brand. Thin flexible plastic strips coated with a peroxide gel are pressed onto the front surfaces of the teeth for a set period each day over a course of one to three weeks.[1][2] They were announced in 2000 and launched to consumers in 2001.[2]

The strips are used to lighten yellowing and surface staining from food, drinks, tobacco and ageing. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article describes strip systems generally as lightening teeth by about one or two shades, with results that vary by starting tooth colour and that can fade over time.[1] Several randomized clinical trials of Crest Whitestrips have been published.[3][4][5]

Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported side effects of peroxide whitening. Regulators treat peroxide strengths differently: the US FDA is described as endorsing gels below 6 percent hydrogen peroxide, while EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent.[1]

paras: The product consists of polyethylene strips coated on one side with a whitening gel whose active ingredient is hydrogen peroxide; other gel components include water, glycerin, carbomer and PVP.[2] Strips come in upper and lower pairs shaped to fit the dental arches.[2] The manufacturer states that the strips are for natural teeth and do not whiten crowns, veneers or fillings.[2]

Variants have included a 6 percent hydrogen peroxide original, a 14 percent Supreme version introduced in 2003, and the 3D line launched in 2010 with an adhesion feature designed to let users talk and drink water while wearing them.[2] Later models added stretchable strips and versions marketed for sensitive teeth or used with an LED light.[2] Treatments in the 3D range run from 30 minutes to an hour per session.[2]

According to a Grokipedia account, a P&G scientist adapted plastic-wrap adhesive technology to hold a thin whitening gel against the teeth. The product was announced in June 2000, offered first through dentists, and went on general sale in May 2001.[2] Wikipedia notes that whitening strips became available in the late 1980s, and that custom-tray bleaching had been introduced by an orthodontist in the late 1960s.[1]

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia describe strips as typically lightening teeth by one or two shades over about two weeks, working best on yellow tones and least well on grey tones.[1] A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 40 adults tested 6 percent hydrogen peroxide Crest Whitestrips used twice daily for six weeks against placebo strips.[4] A separate randomized trial of 50 adults compared Crest Whitestrips with a tray-based system using 3 percent hydrogen peroxide, assessing both instrumental tooth colour and subjective response.[5]

Published human studies of Crest Whitestrips include randomized trials from 2002 to 2009 measuring tooth colour change and colour retention with a 6 percent hydrogen peroxide strip, a six-week placebo-controlled trial in 40 adults, and a 50-adult comparison with a tray system.[3][4][5] A 2004 trial examined a professional-strength strip.[9] The abstracts available describe colour outcomes and safety assessment rather than long-term follow-up.

Wikipedia identifies tooth sensitivity as the most common side effect of peroxide bleaching, with home systems causing less than in-office treatment, and gum irritation or chemical burns as a risk mainly at higher peroxide concentrations or with poorly fitting delivery.[1] Laboratory studies have examined whether strips alter enamel. One in vitro study compared strip, tray and office systems on enamel surfaces, and others used nanoindentation and Raman spectroscopy to assess hardness and composition of tooth tissue after whitening.[6][7][8] A 2004 study evaluated the safety and efficacy of a professional-strength strip.[9] Whitening agents may also affect existing resin restorations, which is the subject of laboratory work on stained composite resins.[10]

As of 2026 the line was described as a leading US at-home whitening brand, with box prices roughly between $20 and $65 depending on the model.[2] Several competing home approaches exist, including custom trays, brush-on gels and whitening rinses, which Wikipedia describes as producing similar or slower results.[1]

card.summary: P&G's over-the-counter peroxide whitening strips; clinical trials show lightening of a shade or two, with sensitivity the usual trade-off.
card.note: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are commonly reported; results can fade.

quick.overview:
Crest Whitestrips are thin plastic strips coated with hydrogen peroxide gel that users stick to their teeth for a set time each day over one to three weeks. They launched in 2001 and are among the best-known at-home whitening products in the US.

Randomized trials exist, and general reviews describe strip systems as lightening teeth by around one or two shades.
quick.mechanism: The peroxide gel oxidises and breaks down stain-causing pigment molecules in and on the enamel, while the adhesive strip holds the gel against the tooth surface.
quick.risks: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects. They are not designed for crowns, veneers or fillings, and regulators differ on allowed peroxide strengths: the EU limits retail products to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.
